title: Nanta
description:
[Performance introduction]

NANTA, a performance created by Korea and highly praised by the world, since 1997

Nanta is a comical depiction of what happens in the kitchen, based on the rhythm of Samulnori, a traditional Korean melody. 
It is Korea's first non-verbal performance.
Kitchen utensils such as knives and cutting boards are sublimated into wonderful musical instruments, creating a spectacular performance, a surprise traditional wedding, and a performance with the audience. 
With dumpling stacking, traditional Korean dance and samgomu harmonizing with the melody, and drumming with a refreshing ending that will make your heart flutter, etc. 
'Nanta' is a powerful performance that can relieve stress in a fun way for people of all ages and genders, regardless of nationality.

title: Tattoo Chronicles Moon Shin Chronology
venue: Gyeongnam | Changwon City Masan Moonshin Art Museum
description: To Moon Jae-in, life was art, and art was life. By following the trajectory of his intense life, we will try to guess the relationship between life and art and the changes in his work over his life. The era in which Moon Jae-in lived was a turbulent period transitioning from modern times to modern times. Let's take a look at the detailed chronology of the life of Moon Jae-in, who, as fate would have it, entered the path of an artist despite the chaotic historical trends such as the Japanese colonial period and liberation, the Korean War, and rapid industrialization. Moon Mun was born on January 16, 1922, in the small city of Takeo, Saga Prefecture, Kyushu, Japan, as the second son of his father, Moon Chan-i, and his mother, Chiwata Taki. His father, who had a free-spirited and pioneering spirit, took the last name of Ahn Chang-nam, a pilot he admired, and gave him the name Moon An-sin (文安信). In 1927, when he was 5 years old, his family moved to Masan, his father's hometown. Soon after, his parents returned to Japan, and he was raised by his grandmother and uncle. When he turned 11, his father settled in Masan alone. At this time, Tattoo separated from his mother. Moon Jae-in, who was especially loved by his father, recalled that his artistic origins were his childhood with his father. Later, the fact that his works were abstract but reminiscent of the vitality (body) of nature was a manifestation of his subconscious as a child, and not only his memories of the sea in Masan with his father, but also his father's attitude toward life, constitutional sincerity, and passionate obsession, which gave him the courage to overcome trials and tribulations, gave him the spiritual foundation and courage to overcome trials. As a teenager, Moon Jae-soo started working at an art studio that deals with foreign masterpieces, and naturally came into contact with art collections of Picasso, Cézanne, and Van Gogh, and imitated numerous masterpieces. In particular, the more he understood Picasso's work, the more he realized that 'originality' was important. Around the age of 16, while secretly planning a trip to Manchuria, he headed to Japan at the recommendation of a friend who visited him. Although he did not want to go to Japan because he longed for and resented his Japanese mother, his determination to study art guided him. While studying at the Japanese Art School, he worked part-time jobs such as theater work, woodworking, and shoe shine to cover tuition, and sent some of the money to his father in Masan to purchase the current art museum site. Moonshin, who returned to Korea with liberation in 1945, holds exhibitions in Masan, Busan, and Seoul. In works such as <Fisherman> (1946), <Red Pepper> (1946), <Fishing> (1948), and <Mountain and Sky> (1948), he boldly expresses the environment in which he lives and the objects produced in that environment with his own colors and shapes. At the <1st Moon Soo-in's Foreign Paintings Solo Exhibition> at Dongwha Gallery in Seoul (1948), critic Gil Jin-seop said, "There is something to be touched by Moon's works." He displays an honest simplicity that can be achieved, and is also highly praised as ‘a writer who has discarded the pretense of old ideas and styles.’ When the Korean War broke out in 1950, he also worked as a war painter and recorded the scenes of the war through <Field Hospital> (1952). Afterwards, he moved his activities to Seoul and participated in the <Modern Art Association> along with Lee Gyu-sang, Han Muk, Yoo Young-guk, Park Go-seok, and Chun Kyeong-ja. This group was formed by mid-career artists in their 30s and 40s with an avant-garde spirit in the national art exhibition and the Korean art world. They put forward the banner of modern art and advocate the purity and uniqueness of art based on their own creative ideology. During this period, tattoos transitioned to abstraction, and the formative experiments pursued by expressionism and cubism can be seen in <Cow> (1957), <Still Life> (1959), and <On Taepyeong-ro> (1959). In 1961, at the age of 39, Moon Shin headed to France. Paris, France, the center of art in the early 20th century, had a free atmosphere that accepted and recognized diversity, and abstract tendencies such as Engformel, Taschism, and neo-realism were dominant. Moon Shin lived in France from 1961 to 1980 (temporarily returning to Korea in 1965-1967). The 1960s was a time when a new art of tattooing was emerging, and people were immersed in the world of abstraction through various experiments with materials and shapes. Such attempts also appear in <Love> (1962), <Untitled> (1964), and <Sculpture on which humans can live> (1966-1967), which crosses the boundaries between sculpture and space. In 1967, Moon Jae-in participated in the International Sculpture Symposium, with gallerist John Craven serving as commissioner.

title: The New, The Crafts: Put your heart, connect your hearts
description: ○ The Korean Traditional Culture Center special exhibition at Incheon International Airport Terminal 2, 『The New, The Crafts』, focuses on the values ​​of harmony and coexistence and introduces works that reinterpret Korean traditional crafts in a modern way. The formative language of traditional crafts, called ‘joining’, ‘weaving’, and ‘containing’, is revived as a symbol that connects the past and present, myself and others. Participating artists explain the values ​​of tradition accumulated over a long period of time from their own perspectives, and contain positive energy and warm messages about life in their author's notes. We hope that many people visiting the airport will respect each other's differences through this exhibition, have the experience of sharing their hearts through works of art, and experience relaxation within it. ○ East Building: (Traditional Crafts) ‘Containing the Heart’ - Composed of works by artists who work on moon jars and utensils, lacquerware and mother-of-pearl lacquerware, which are representative works of art that preserve Korean beauty - Participating artists: Seoul City Intangible Heritage painter Daehyun Son, metal craft Seo Do-sik, metal craft Hyunju Kim ○ West Building: (Contemporary art) ‘Connecting Hearts’ - Leeumgwa A modern reinterpretation of traditional crafts that highlight the beauty of weaving, produced by contemporary artists who unfold their own artist notes - Participating artists: Textile Kang Geum-seong, Textile Lee Hye-min, Installation Hong Seong-cheol ※ This exhibition is held within the duty-free area of Incheon International Airport Passenger Terminal 2 and can be viewed upon departure. venue: Jeju | Jeju Provincial Museum of Art
description: The courtyard project “Space Tree” outdoor exhibition uses the space tree, a symbol that often appears in ancient mythology and religion, as its motif. The common appearance of this concept in various cultures can be seen as a common expression of the way humans try to understand the structure of nature and the universe. The exhibition theme, “Connection between Heaven and Earth,” symbolically connects the visible and the invisible. It is also an attempt to cross the boundaries between life and death, time and memory, and humans and the universe. This tree standing in space is a visible object and an axis of unique thought. title: Manin Mountain: Records of Preservation and Deconstruction
description: National Folk Museum Paju is hosting the conservation science exhibition “Maninsan: Records of Preservation and Deconstruction.” Man-in-san (萬人傘) is a type of Il-san (日傘), and can be said to be a souvenir gifted by the people of the village as a token of gratitude to a leader who conducted a benevolent government when he leaves the village. The National Folk Museum of Korea possesses a total of 5 pieces of Maninsan, and starting with conservation treatment for exhibition in 2006, conservation treatment for all 5 pieces has been completed by 2024. This exhibition introduces two pieces of Maninsan, and in particular, Maninsan by Lee Jong-seung (李鍾承, 1828~?), a Gwanseo military commander, is being presented to the public for the first time after conservation treatment. We hope that you will take time to think about the meaning of preserving cultural heritage through the preservation process of Maninsan Mountain. The performance/exhibition program may change depending on the circumstances of the organizer, performer, etc. 1688-2220

title: The life story of Seocheon Tidal Flat: The sea beneath the wings
venue: Chungnam | National Marine Biological Resources Center Securium
description: To commemorate its 10th anniversary, the National Marine Biological Resources Center is exhibiting “The Sea Under the Wings - Life Story of the Seocheon Tidal Flat” in the special exhibition room on the 3rd floor of the Securium. Seocheon’s mudflats were listed as a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site on July 26, 2021 as part of ‘Korean Tidal Flasts’. This exhibition was prepared to publicize the outstanding ecological value of the Seocheon Tidal Flat and the importance of mudflat conservation, and in particular, to introduce its role as a major stopping point for endangered migratory birds. Starting with the Yubudo mudflat video, the exhibition is organized into four major themes: ▲Korea's mudflats ▲Biological diversity of the Seocheon mudflats ▲Waterfowl of the Seocheon mudflats ▲Seocheon mudflats and humans. You can view actual specimens of over 50 different species of waterfowl, including endangered species, and also observe enlarged models of small creatures such as midges living in the mudflats. We also created a space where visitors can experience hands-on activities such as taking pictures and putting together puzzles in the mud flat. We hope that this exhibition will provide an opportunity to once again feel that the Seocheon Tidal Flat is a valuable heritage to be passed on to future generations. The performance/exhibition program may change depending on the circumstances of the organizer, performer, etc. 1688-2220

title: A memorable moment of 80 years of walking together
description: Buyeo National Museum is holding a special exhibition, “80 Years of Memories Walking Together,” to commemorate its 80th anniversary. Buyeo National Museum opened as the Buyeo branch of the National Museum on October 13, 1945, and reopened in 1971 by constructing a new building behind Buyeo Guest House on Busosan Mountain. It was moved to its current location on Geumseongsan Mountain on August 6, 1993. This special exhibition divides the history of the Buyeo National Museum into the Japanese colonial period, Busosan 1st period, Busosan 2nd period, and Geumseongsan period and systematically displays the main contents so that the museum can understand and empathize with the path taken over time. Part 1, Japanese Colonial Period, exhibited materials left by the Buyeo Historic Sites Preservation Society and the Buyeo branch of the Japanese Government General Museum to examine the perception of Buyeo at the time and the nature of the exhibition. Part 2, Busosan 1, contains the story of the first director Hong Sa-jun and his staff's efforts to lay the foundation for the museum in various fields such as securing collections, exhibitions, and academic research. Part 3, Busosan 2nd phase, introduced exhibitions and academic research activities that became more active after the construction of Busosan's new building, and helped understanding with a kiosk video that reproduced the permanent exhibition at the time. Returning to Buyeo after a long time, the traditional bronze sword and bronze ax form excavated from the Songguk-ri ruins in Buyeo welcome visitors. Part 4, Geumseongsan Period, clearly organizes the excavation, preservation, and exhibition records of the Baekje gilt-bronze incense burner, and examines the museum's growth as a Baekje specialty museum by holding various special exhibitions. Part 5, The Museum in My Life, contains the stories of people who have formed a relationship with the museum, and is comprised of a participatory exhibition decorated with ‘Museum and Me’ interview videos and photos submitted to the ‘Looking for Photos’ event, adding to the meaning of the 80th anniversary. We hope you will reminisce about the 80 years of Buyeo National Museum and join us for the next 80 years by viewing this special exhibition prepared to commemorate the 80th anniversary of its opening. title: Spreading and Remaining: Jang Ucchin’s ink painting
venue: game | Yangju City Chang Ucchin Museum of Art
description: <Spreading and Remaining: Jang Ucchin's Ink Paintings> was planned to expand the scope of Jang Ucchin's research, which had focused on oil paintings, and to strengthen the research function of the collection. In particular, this exhibition sheds new light on the value of Jang Ucchin's ink paintings based on the research results of <Seeing Jang Ucchin Again>, an academic conference commemorating the 10th anniversary of the museum's opening. Jang Ucchin's ink paintings were produced in large numbers around 1980, and are a genre that represents Jang Ucchin's art world, along with oil paintings and magic paintings. Like ink painting, ink painting uses ink and paper as materials, but it is different in that it reinterprets the symbolic materials that appear in traditional ink painting in terms of content and form. Art historian Choi Gyeong-hyeon commented at an academic conference, “Although the artist used traditional materials such as paper, brush, and ink, he did not want to make a dichotomous distinction between Western and Oriental paintings, so he made it clear that it was a new genre,” which clearly shows the originality of ink paintings. This exhibition examines the influence of Ucchin Jang's ink paintings on his overall artistic world by dividing them into three subjects: folk painting, Buddhism, and daily life. These three materials appear repeatedly in the work and provide important clues to understanding Jang Ucchin's worldview. In this exhibition, which will feature about 40 works, including collections that have not been revealed to the public, the art historical value and unique beauty of ink paintings will be confirmed. title: MMCA Overseas Masterpiece: Water Lilies and Chandelier
venue: game | National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Gwacheon
description: Collections are important assets of an art museum that reveal the flow of art and history of an era. Disclosing and sharing collected objects is an important role of contemporary art museums and is deeply related to their essential function. The ‘Room of Curiosities’ in 16th-century Europe, which is considered to be the origin of the art museum, is a space that provides new experiences and intellectual exploration to viewers by displaying rare and exotic collections. With the formation of modern nation-states, publicness expanded and artworks that had been privately owned were opened to the public and gradually developed into modern museums. Like the Room of Curiosity, this exhibition is a permanent exhibition that introduces about 40 works carefully selected from the international art collection collected by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art to encourage new experiences and intellectual exploration. In particular, through the acquisition of the Lee Kun-hee Collection in 2021, you can take a look at not only 19th-century European art housed in the museum, but also various overseas works of art that have expanded the boundaries of modern art. The mutually disparate words ‘Water Lilies and Chandelier’ used as the title of the exhibition are a combination of the titles of “Pond with Water Lilies” (1917-1920), a work by Claude Monet, a light painter representing the 19th century impressionism, and “Black Chandelier” (2017-2021), a work by Ai Weiwei, a world-renowned artist active in the same era. The conjunctive particle ‘-and’ is used between ‘water lily’, which refers to nature, and the artificial object ‘chandelier’, to convey the meaning of creating the possibility of another connection beyond eras and boundaries. If you listen to the various scenes of overseas art in the 100 years between the creation of the two works and imagine their relationships, you will soon reach a time of new experiences full of curiosity. title: AI-based media art exhibition 《New-Media Disaster-Interpretation》
description: 《Disaster-Interpretation of New-Media》 Today, ‘artificial intelligence (AI)’ goes beyond a simple tool and operates as a medium that reorganizes not only daily life but also art. Technologies such as multimodal processing, interactivity, and deep learning are changing the way we sense and fundamentally shaking up the structure of creation and reception. Art is no longer a fixed result, but begins to work again under new conditions created by AI. Marshall McLuhan, a media theorist in the 1960s, argued that “media is a message,” and viewed media as an environment that reorganizes human senses and social structures. After radio, telephone, and the Internet, today's AI has emerged as a new media that most clearly reveals this logic. The exhibition “Disaster-Interpretation of New Media” explores this very point. Here, ‘disaster’ refers to a crack and shock to the existing order, and ‘reinterpretation’ refers to a new possibility (environment) discovered in the gap. This exhibition reveals scenes of this transition through four works. 《New World? II》 visualizes NFT's real-time data as an image of a wave, revealing the invisible flow of technology and environmental implications. 《Electric Dream》 explores the boundaries between memory and identity through the interaction between AI images and visitors. 《Ludenstopia》 reinterprets real space and play space by AI and reconstructs it into a third imaginary space. “Everything is Connected” rethinks the relationship between technology, nature, and humans through ecosystem and historical data. In this environment, the artist changes from being a being who presents a conclusion to a being who designs the conditions of the question, and the viewer responds to the question and becomes a new sensory subject. 《Disaster-Interpretation of New-Media》 examines these changes in sense and interpretation and explores new ways in which art operates today. title: Conservation science, a new beginning, a future together
description: Museums are spaces where human heritage spanning thousands of years meets us today. Behind that encounter is ‘conservation science’ that touches the traces of time and connects the past, present, and future. The history of conservation science at the National Museum of Korea first began in 1976. It started out in a harsh environment where foreign substances were removed and glue was applied with a single toothpick to attach broken pieces of pottery or broken gilt-bronze Buddha statues, but it has now developed into a specialized field that scientifically diagnoses materials, production techniques, and current conditions to find the most appropriate preservation method. Today's conservation science is intertwined with new technologies called digital and artificial intelligence (AI). We aim to open a new future for museum conservation science by converting the conservation processing technology, 3D scanning, high-resolution images and analysis data that we have accumulated over the past 50 years into digital materials and applying artificial intelligence. Conservation science is a science that does not just leave behind the legacy of ancient mankind, but also reveals traces of life and wisdom contained within it and passes it on to future generations. The National Museum of Korea's conservation science is at the center of the way to preserve our cultural heritage for past, present, and future generations. title: Waking up from the dirt of Sangwonsa Temple in Yeoju
description: There have long been traces of what is believed to be a temple site on Hyemoksan Mountain in Yeoju. Only the podium stone and absence of the pagoda from the remaining building site showed traces of the past, but the identity of the place was not clearly known. Yeoju City, together with the National Heritage Administration, commissioned the Buddhist Cultural Heritage Research Institute and conducted an excavation survey for five years starting in 2020. As a result, it was revealed that this temple site was Sangwonsa Temple, where Zen Master Hyeonwook stayed at the end of the Unified Silla Dynasty and was operated until the late Joseon Dynasty. Yeoju Museum is holding a special exhibition titled “Yeoju Sangwonsa Temple, Awakening from the Soil” to examine the appearance of Sangwonsa Temple through the relics and relics identified during the excavation of the Sangwonsa Temple Site. We will be shown the forgotten scenery of Sangwonsa Temple through excavation work and relics such as roof tiles, celadon, and white porcelain. Sangwonsa finally woke up after sleeping in the dirt for a long time. Please listen to the story of Sangwonsa, prepared with excitement as if opening an old time capsule. title: A special exhibition <Hello, Geumseongdang> to meet the original form of Korean shamanism
description: The exhibition title 『Hello, Geumseongdang』 is a warm greeting to the relics that have returned after wandering for a long time, and also contains the hope that Geumseongdang will continue to live peacefully with the local community in the future. Geumseongdang, located in Jingwan-dong, Eunpyeong-gu, Seoul, is a national folk cultural heritage site where the royal family and the civilians held rituals together in the late Joseon Dynasty. It is a place where exorcisms were performed with King Geumseong and Grand Prince Geumseong as the main deity. During the development of Eunpyeong New Town, the Geumseongdang building was preserved, but the internal relics were deposited at the Seoul Museum of History and returned to the Eunpyeong History Hanok Museum through donation in the fall of 2024. The exhibition consists of three themes: ‘Look – Do – Share’. I hope that this exhibition will be a meaningful opportunity to reflect on the true meaning of shamanism, which has been neglected due to misunderstanding and indifference, and to reconnect with relics that have been returned to their original places after a long period of time. title: Kim Heung-soo: The first month of aesthetics
venue: Jeju | Jeju Museum of Contemporary Art
description: 《The Sun and Moon of Aesthetics》 is the exhibition title inspired by an article written by Kim Heung-soo (1919-2014) in 『Shindonga』 in 1980. This exhibition sheds light on the life and art world of an artist who explored ‘beauty’ throughout his life through never-before-seen works and various archives. Kim Heung-soo lived in Japan (1938-1944), France (1955-1961), and the United States (1967-1982), and in 1977, he advocated his own formative language, “Yin-Yang Formative Harmonism.” We take a look at the process through which his artistic world was formed through paintings, drawings, collages, posters, photographs, and contributions. In the permanent exhibition room, we look back on Kim Heung-soo's life through works and archives. The artist leaves behind his or her work, and the archive surrounds the work and reveals the texture of life. We follow Kim Heung-soo's journey to find his unique artistic language in his footsteps from Japan to Paris and the United States. In the special exhibition room, we focus on Kim Heung-soo's drawings. You can see in one place the Jeju Museum of Modern Art's collection, the original illustrations for his contributions, portrait drawings, and even nude drawings that are essential to his art. Heungsu Kim's drawings greet us at the starting line of creation and allow us to feel the artist's thoughts and concerns up close. Through this exhibition, I hope you will pause and look at the question, ‘What is beauty?’ The performance/exhibition program may change depending on the circumstances of the organizer, performer, etc. 1688-2220

title: Seoul Living Center Museum Special Exhibition <Welcoming the Baby>
description: The Seoul Living History Museum holds an exhibition every year to remember and record the rapidly changing lifestyles of people in modern Seoul and share them with citizens. In particular, we are sequentially holding exhibitions that introduce how the lives of people in Seoul have changed over time by life cycle, including marriage, birth, childcare, and education. This time, we prepared a special exhibition, “Welcoming the Baby,” with the theme of changes in the pregnancy and birth culture of Seoul citizens. How has the pregnancy and birth culture of Seoul citizens changed from the 1950s to today, after the joy of liberation and the horrors of war? This exhibition, inspired by the late author Park Wan-seo's picture book 『Meeting the Baby』, sought to shed a warm light on the moments in Seoul when people wait and welcome new life in their daily lives. The 5th Hangul Experiment Project <Writing (character) sense (gak): writing and tools>
description: Depending on what letters are used and where they are used, the unique properties of the material leave traces. Additionally, depending on who writes, the movements of the body and mind are revealed in a unique form called handwriting. All of these things create the ‘texture of letters.’ The 5th Hangul Experiment Project <Writing(character) Sense(Gak): Writing and Tools> examines the relationship between writing and tools from various angles in the process leading to ‘writing-tool-action’. This exhibition is an experimental attempt to cross the boundaries of body, function, and materiality by converting tools into senses. It further raises questions about how new tools such as artificial intelligence (AI) will change the way we write. Writing is the starting point for creating the formative rules of letters and the process of recording the fundamental human impulse toward self-discovery and self-understanding. Tools used in this recording process include physical media that enable writing, such as brushes, pens, and digital styluses, and all media that record. Visual elements such as the shape, size, arrangement, and margins of letters created through writing are conveyed as a holistic sense through reading. The material properties of tools directly affect the texture and form of letters. The 23 teams of writers and designers sought to leave traces with their own tools and find the meaning and sense of writing. This exhibition focuses on newly discovering the textual texture and linguistic and design value of Hangul. title: Joan Jonas: The World Beyond Man
venue: game | Nam June Paik Art Center
description: The 8th Nam June Paik Art Award winner's exhibition, Joan Jonas: The World Beyond Humans, is the first solo exhibition of Joan Jonas (1936-, USA) held at a domestic art museum. Joan Jonas is a world-renowned artist who has pioneered her own genre across a variety of media, including video, performance, and drawing, for over 50 years from the 1960s to the present. From performance and video to conceptual art and theater, his experimental works have had a significant impact on the combination and expansion of various genres in modern art. This exhibition is organized according to his creative trajectory throughout his life, from his early representative work “Wind” (1968), which experiments with the interaction between nature and the human body, to “Empty Rooms” (2025), which visualizes the sense of absence and loss by combining sculpture, video, and drawing. The first chapter of the exhibition highlights Joan Jonas' role as a pioneer in the performance and video genres through works developed based on New York society and artist communities in the 1960s and 1970s. The second chapter focuses on the author's experiments in building a new ecological narrative based on mythology and literature, breaking away from human-centered narratives in earnest starting in the 1980s. The third chapter presents the author's latest work, focusing on how visual elements that appear repeatedly from the early 1960s to 2025 are changing and expanding, as well as showing the author's perspective on contemporary issues. This solo exhibition by Joan Jonas will recall the meaning of the Nam June Paik Art Award, which is awarded to “artists who have contributed to human peace and left a mark in art history,” and will provide time for reflection on “the world beyond humans.” The performance/exhibition program may change depending on the circumstances of the organizer, performer, etc. 1688-2220

title: Chuncheon National Museum Brand 2 ‘Gangwon’s Buddhist art, the path to enlightenment’
description: Chuncheon National Museum opens a new permanent exhibition hall brand 2, ‘Gangwon’s Buddhist Art, The Path to Enlightenment.’ Gangwon's clean nature is suitable for Buddhist practice to wash away suffering and seek enlightenment. Since Goguryeo accepted Buddhism in 372, Buddhist buildings and works of art have been produced throughout the country. The earliest records of Buddhism in the Gangwon region are related to Silla. Famous monks from the Silla Dynasty left traces at Geumgangsan Mountain, Odaesan Mountain, and Naksansa Temple. Buddhist culture flourished in Gangwon, following Unified Silla's Gyeongju and nearby areas. During the Goryeo Dynasty, large-scale temples were built around Wonju. You can see various aspects of Gangwon Buddhist art through the large Buddha statue made of iron and stone in Wonju and the Tibetan Buddhist style Bodhisattva statue on Mt. Geumgang. The central temples of the region, such as Woljeongsa Temple and Yujeomsa Temple, maintained their legacy even during the Joseon Dynasty. Traces of Buddhist art can be found throughout Gangwon and in museums. In this newly created exhibition hall, we will use Buddhist ritual tools and Buddhist sculptures to explore in depth what the ‘enlightened’ Buddha realized, how he puts it into practice, and what the world of enlightenment is like. As we move toward enlightenment, we hope to face pain and ultimately reach a time of peace and freedom from suffering. The performance/exhibition program may change depending on the circumstances of the organizer, performer, etc. 1688-2220

title: The story of modern Daegu electricity - From Daegu Electric to Daeheung Electric -
description: This small exhibition, which examines what changes occurred when electricity was introduced to Daegu, began with the record that ‘electricity began to be supplied to Daegu on January 1, 1913, and lights were turned on at night.’ This study was designed to find out how electricity was supplied to Daegu and what changes occurred in Daegu society. In the exhibition, you can see the Daegu Modern History Museum's collection of 『Daeheung Electric Co., Ltd. History』 (1939), photo postcards, and graduation albums. You can learn about the establishment and growth of the electric company in Daegu through various photos, newspaper articles, and advertisements from the time, and see the night view of modern Daegu through photo postcards and graduation albums. title: Nomads on the Road: The Legacy of Movement and Exchange in Central Asia
description: 《Nomad on the Road》 is the second permanent exhibition at the ACC Asian Culture Museum, following 《The World Opened by Monsoon》. This exhibition introduces the cultural heritage that blossomed in grasslands and oasis cities, following the footsteps of caravans (caravans) that traveled through Central Asia. The main characters of the exhibition are two types of ‘nomads’. One is a mobile merchant who left traces of exchanges between the caravanserai (merchants' accommodation) and the bazaar (market), and the other is a nomad of the grasslands who moved according to the rhythm of nature and lived with minimal traces. Their movements piled up one by one to form the Silk Road. The Silk Road was not one road, but many paths created by the traces of countless steps, departures, and stays. In the exhibition, you can see the heritage of Central Asia's movements and exchanges, including exquisite miniature paintings and ceramics, colorful textiles and carpets, nomadic horse decorations and yurts. The road still continues in our footsteps. We invite you to the traces of time engraved on the road and the stories of people traveling to and from the city. title: Sangho Shin: Infinite Variation
venue: game | National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Gwacheon
description: Shin Sang-ho (1947~) has responded to changes in society and art since the 1960s and has built his own artistic world using clay as a medium. He is a representative artist who has led Korean modern ceramics with various ceramic forms and excellent technical skills supporting them. In the 1960s, he started his career in ceramics by operating a wood-fired kiln in Icheon, Gyeonggi-do and making traditional ceramics. Since then, he has expanded the boundaries of ceramics in accordance with changes of the times and his inner artistic curiosity, unfolding the world of clay in a variety of ways. The exhibition title «Shin Sang-ho: Infinite Variations» symbolizes the artist's continuous journey of deconstructing the traditional form and meaning of Korean ceramics while simultaneously establishing a new order. Shin Sang-ho sought his identity as a craftsman and industrial force by producing traditional ceramics during a time when national values ​​were emphasized in the era of industrial advancement. In the wave of internationalization around the 1988 Seoul Olympics, he boldly went beyond the traditional norms of ceramic art and pioneered a new genre of ceramic sculpture. Since then, in the 21st century, an era of diversification and hybridity, he has continued to make open and convergent attempts to cross the boundaries between art and architecture through ceramic installation and architectural ceramic work. Furthermore, in the 2020s, he presented ceramic paintings by again subversively thinking about clay, which he had been exploring for a long time. He has expanded the horizons of domestic modern ceramics, maintained a liberal attitude and experimental spirit as an artist, and drawn a trajectory of constant challenge. This exhibition is comprised of a total of five parts according to the development of the times, and introduces the artist's wide creative spectrum, ranging from traditional ceramics to ceramic sculpture, architectural ceramics, objects combined with other media, and ceramic paintings. title: Room of Water Drops: 3D2D
venue: Jeju | Jeju Provincial Kim Chang-yeol Museum of Art
description: This exhibition is the third in the ‘Room of Water Drops’ series, which focuses on three-dimensional works from the Kim Chang-yeol Museum’s collection. Using various locations, including the first exhibition room and the hallway, we look at a journey that crosses the border between two-dimensional and three-dimensional through works that have been revealed and not previously revealed. Kim Tschang-yeol began taking interest in three-dimensional objects in the 1980s. Having tried various media such as canvas, wooden boards, paper, and newspaper for his paintings, he explored the possibilities of three-dimensional work in 1986 by presenting a work in which two circular glass spheres filled with water were placed on a cushion. Three-dimensional experiments, which had been halted for a while, resumed in earnest in the 1990s. With the realization that “there are insurmountable limits in two-dimensional paintings,” Kim Tschang-yeol attempted to expand space by creating water drop-shaped glass and placing it in a box with a thousand character inscription or installing it on a sand pyramid. In this exhibition, archived videos of Kim Tschang-yeol's three-dimensional and installation works will also be released. For the first time, this is an opportunity to see the artistic journey of ‘Water Drop Painter’ Kim Tschang-yeol, who went beyond two dimensions and into three dimensions. The exhibition talks about how much effort was put into the birth of a child, both then and now. We prepared this exhibition to share our view of childbirth as not just a number, but as a miraculous moment when life is born. title: 《Electric Shock》
venue: Seoul | Seoul Museum of Buk Seoul Museum of Art
description: 《Electric Shock》 is a report on ‘electricity’. Electricity is ‘the totality of energy generated through electrons’ and is an important resource that operates modern society. From home appliances used in everyday life to digital consumption, advanced production lines and logistics systems, it is not easy to imagine life without electricity. The recent commercialization of artificial intelligence (AI) and the expansion of big tech companies are exponentially increasing power consumption. In order to quickly adopt cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, how to secure and supply electricity reliably has emerged as the most important issue, and this has begun to determine the competitiveness of countries and companies. The so-called ‘era of electric hegemony’ has begun, and along with the endless desire for technological development, various efforts are being made to develop electric power within limited resources. Electricity is no longer an energy source that enriches daily life, but has become an essential weapon that determines survival. This thirst is causing indiscriminate development, and even the efforts made for carbon neutrality are turning into romantic promises that delay technological development. Self-reflective movements that called for ‘sustainable’ coexistence, such as post-humanism, the Anthropocene, and humans and non-humans, are disappearing into history already written in the “electric war” unfolding right before our eyes. 《Electric Shock》 traces the acute relationship between technology and the environment that actually occurs today by revealing it as a circuit called electricity. The performance/exhibition program may change depending on the circumstances of the organizer, performer, etc. 1688-2220

title: Artist's Study 《Unfinished Botanical Paper - Soyo Lee》《Flower Clock-Anna Riddler》
venue: Seoul | Seoul Museum of Buk Seoul Museum of Art
description: The ‘Artist’s Research’ series of the Buk Seoul Museum of Art, ‘Unfinished Botanical Paper – Soyo Lee’ and ‘Flower Clock – Anna Riddler’, is an exhibition that introduces the creative world based on the research of artists, elaborately constructed in an original way that crosses various academic and technological fields such as art history, natural history, biology, geography, and artificial intelligence. The authors do not treat research simply as an auxiliary element to creation, but show how research and creation work together as a closely interlocked axis. The research-creation axis intersects with the art-academic and art-technology axes, which are other axes brought about by the work of connecting art with other fields. 《Unfinished Botanical Journal - Lee So-yo》 presents the research-based art of Lee So-yo, who has continued to create creations that mediate art and scientific knowledge and fuse art and academia, through <『Korean Plant Illustrator Poisonous Plants』, Annotations>. The 『Poisonous Plants of the Korean Peninsula』 written by Do Bong-seop and Shim Hak-jin, who attempted to compile the plants of the Korean Peninsula through direct observation and collection, was a step toward compilation of the Korean Peninsula's flora, and was created together by many researchers at the time and later. It is incomplete knowledge. Soyo Lee participated in the artist's research and has been exploring the dissemination and movement of plant knowledge contained in this book and the formation of vegetation zones that exist outside the book for several years. He added visual annotations by implementing the collected plants and research materials into installation art works processed into preserved materials and drawings. Through this, Soyo Lee's research-based art, which explores the creation and flow of knowledge by conducting document analysis and field research, is revealed in detail. 《Flower Clock - Anna Ridler》 explores the intersection of critical vision and sensuous beauty where technology, nature, and art intersect, and sheds light on the research-based creative world of Anna Ridler, who is attracting attention for her new artistic practice of creation using artificial intelligence data sets. The works introduced in this exhibition are inspired by the 18th century biologist Carl Linnaeus' concept of the 'flower clock', and are works that visualize the flow of time constructed by humans, such as 24 hours or a year, through the physiological rhythm of flowers that bloom and fall at specific times of the day. This series, which explores the relationship between 'inhuman temporality', the way non-human beings perceive and maintain time, and human clock time, unfolds Anna Ridler's side as an artist and researcher who seeks another way to understand the world and reconsiders the meaning of nature, humanity, sense and perception in the digital age. title: Dopamine Hype Dopamine Hype
description: ⟪Dopamine Hype⟫ explores the pleasure, addiction, insensitivity, and choice created by dopamine in modern society through the collaboration of art and science. Artist Soyoung Jeong and scientist Jaeseon Jang present in an installation how the brain's prediction process and dopamine circulation affect desire and free will. Eobchae and scientist Choi Sang-guk warn of the social ramifications of dopamine addiction by revealing the connection between technology, war, and nervous system desensitization. Moojin Brothers interprets the emotional amplitude between disaster and pleasure as the duality of dopamine, while Dapertutto Studio views ‘addiction’ as a device, not a disease, and implements it in a theatrical form by comparing it to the body. This exhibition presents new insights through the convergence of art and science, and illuminates in a multi-layered manner how dopamine reorganizes human behavior and society as a whole. title: 'Invisible Actors'
description: Artist Gyeongjae Cho is a photographer who completed his studies at the Meisterschuller University of Fine Arts in Münster and has been active in Europe and Korea. Within the camera's limited field of view, he creates real spaces as if they were abstract paintings and records them in photographs. Cho Kyungjae’s work focuses on delicate exploration of space, objects, light and time. He utilizes a variety of media experiments, including installation and performance, with a focus on photography. He rearranges and re-stages everyday objects and spaces to capture the moments we often pass by and the agency of beings. In particular, his work abstractly reconstructs and records spaces and objects within a limited field of view, revealing subtle interactions and inherent changes between objects, space, and time. He also carefully observes the interaction between space, objects, and time, and the results of this exploration are reflected in his photographic work. His photographs do not use collage or digital editing, but are pure photographs taken with an analog camera using real spaces and physical objects installed. In this process, the object loses its original function and form and is transformed into the material's unique color and form, creating a new visual language. In this exhibition “Invisible Actors,” this exploration is revealed through the ‘play of invisible actors’ unfolding within the camera, showing that existence itself is already an act. Through the work, audiences can directly experience the subtle interaction of objects, space, and time. Through exhibitions, Cho Kyung-jae has continued to attempt to expand his photography work into various physical media such as installation and sound, rather than remaining in a completed form in itself. As in his previous exhibitions, this exhibition also shows the process of transforming and deconstructing the structural characteristics of photographic work into different formats. Cho Kyung-jae ‘Invisible Actors’ Jo Kyung-jae’s photos resemble a stage. And there are no actors on the stage. Instead, objects, light, and the flow of time are assigned their own roles and quietly create a scene. The artist follows the process of changing light throughout the day and carefully observes the landscape where the light falls on objects. The moments he captures are not completed plays, but are closer to ongoing rehearsals or fleeting conversations in which light speaks to objects. If you look at his photos for a long time, a subtle grouping of objects appears, as if they were placed with awareness of each other. While there is an orderly alignment of lines and angles precisely, there is also an indirect grouping that creates relationships by reacting to each other without disturbing the unique properties of each object. These two movements are static on the outside, but internally they create slow waves like signals that coordinate the scene. Under Gyeongjae Cho’s gaze, objects are not objects that simply reflect light. They push and pull the scenery in a lighted space and quietly adjust their positions like performers who recognize others on stage. Through these scenes, the author reveals that the fact that an object ‘exists’ is already an act. At that moment, the camera is not just a recording device, but an invisible observer and audience, and a mediator of the subtle tension between light and objects. So while his photos remind us of an empty stage, they also leave the impression that invisible actors are constantly reacting to each other and creating their own scenes. The scene is not a fixed image, but is closer to a small rehearsal created by light, objects, distances, and angles working together. At this point, it is natural to understand that Cho Kyung-jae's photographs resemble a stage. This is not an imitation of a theatrical device, but because the sum of the order, tension, and relationships already flowing between objects constitutes a stage. title: JMA Outdoor Garden Project 《Sun Setting in the South》

description: The new JMA outdoor garden project “Sun Setting in the South” looks again at beings that have not been recognized in everyday life and explores the possibility of forming new relationships outside the framework of familiar senses. The works make us rethink the places we have passed by and open our eyes to things that were previously invisible. In this exhibition, the works are placed in a space that has not been given special meaning, allowing viewers to naturally form relationships with the works and participate in the situation through chance encounters. Works placed in a loose and open manner instead of a fixed structure allow familiar places to be experienced differently, blurring the boundaries divided by the existing order. Participating artists Kang Yong-myeon, Kim Young-bong, Moon Min, Lee Kang-won, and Chae Seung-seung reveal invisible beings and places in these local conditions through their own words. This goes beyond simple discovery and allows us to sense the process by which meaning is formed and transformed, and leads us to imagine another possibility of coexistence. title: Deep Affection
venue: Gyeongnam | Changwon City Masan Moonshin Art Museum
description: “If there is something I am obsessed with, it is my love for living things in nature. I know that the love for living things in nature is eternal and will continue until the day this earth disappears.” - Moon Shin - This exhibition examines the representative works of artist Shin Moon, housed at the Moonshin Art Museum, under the theme of ‘love.’ Moon Shin (1922-1995) never lost the feeling of ‘love’ despite the loneliness of living in a foreign country for a long time, intense creative activities, and overwhelming daily life. He has always been obsessed with love for living things in nature and said that if you cannot feel the emotion of love in your work, it is just an ornament. Although he was a quiet person who always created in silence and rarely revealed his feelings, Moon Jae-in's passionate passion and deep love for art remained constant throughout his life. The feeling of love contained in the tattoo extended to his hometown Masan, his homeland, his father and those around him, peace, nature and life, and the universe, and became the driving force and theme of his art. His works, housed at the Moonshin Art Museum, always shine toward the universe while looking at the nature of his hometown, which he loved. I hope it will be a meaningful time for you to feel the love that Moon Moon felt and to look at his work with loving eyes. title: 16th Special Exhibition 『Women Lead Life!: Love & Dedication』
venue: Chungbuk | Ban Ki-moon Peace Memorial Hall
description: The 8th UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon Peace Memorial Hall held the 16th special exhibition, “Women Leading Life: Love & Dedication.” We introduce about 30 pieces of the collection, including paintings and sculptures on the theme of women, that former Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon received from heads of state and organizations during his term as UN Secretary-General (2007-2016). These collections express the international community's deep sympathy and gratitude for the president's efforts to promote women's human rights. This exhibition introduces works that depict the ordinary daily lives and aspirations of women around the world. It sheds light on their strong and beautiful lives, overcoming adversity and leading themselves and the world with love and devotion to their families. In addition, we introduce the activities and achievements of former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, who has led the way in improving women's human rights and gender equality. During his tenure, former Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon emphasized that "sustainable development and peace are impossible without guaranteeing women's rights." In particular, he actively supported women's participation in education and economic activities and led international cooperation to eradicate violence against women. Although international organizations and private organizations, including the United Nations, are making efforts in various ways to promote women's human rights and eliminate gender discrimination, gender discrimination still exists in complex forms in our society. Many women around the world silently bear their social responsibilities as daughters, wives, and mothers, and protect the lives of themselves and their communities without losing passion and hope. Rather than grand discourse, this exhibition seeks to capture the moments of women quietly living their daily lives to form new perspectives and deep empathy. We hope you will join us on this great and brilliant journey of life to see how their dedicated love and passion have led their lives and created a better future for humanity. title: Special exhibition commemorating the 80th anniversary of liberation <Reclaiming History 1945-1948, Back to Us>
venue: Seoul | National Museum of Korean History
description: In 2025, as we celebrate the 80th anniversary of liberation, we reconsider the meaning of ‘recovery.’ The three years of liberation from liberation in 1945 to the establishment of the government in 1948 were not simply a period of escape from Japanese colonial rule, but an intense journey to recover our lost name, correct distorted history, and restore our words, culture, and memories. It was also a time to reaffirm the identity of ‘me and us’ by deciding on an anniversary to remember together. This exhibition highlights the passionate efforts to regain our integrity in the turbulent space of liberation. Please take a look at what it was like at that time, when we were full of expectations for a new country and a desire to return to ‘us again.’ The performance/exhibition program may change depending on the circumstances of the organizer, performer, etc. 1688-2220

title: Special exhibition at Hanbat Education Museum commemorating 30 years of education reform [Today’s education, future drawn by the past]
description: Education has responded to changes in the times. In the late 2010s, software (SW) education and artificial intelligence (AI) education began in line with the trend of the ‘4th Industrial Revolution’ era, and artificial intelligence has now become part of everyday life. In 1995, 30 years ago, the May 31 Education Reform was promoted to prepare for the globalization and information age of the 21st century and create an education that was completely different from before. This special exhibition focuses on changes in school settings led by major policies of education reform. This change is the ‘future education’ designed 30 years ago and is the foundation of the education we experience today. Therefore, evaluation of the achievements and limitations of education reform is currently ongoing. I hope you take the time to look back at the starting point of today’s education and think about what the ‘future education’ we are creating is and what it should be like. title: 2025 Atelier Gwanghwa Winter Exhibition [Emerging Artist Contest]
《Choi Jae-eun: Promise》
description: The Seoul Museum of Art is hosting 《Choi Jae-eun: Where Beings Be》 as a solo exhibition by a representative contemporary art artist. Jae-eun Choi (born in 1953) is an artist who has uniquely illuminated the relationship between life and nature in multi-layered time and space, encompassing a variety of media and areas such as sculpture, video, installation, and architecture. Choi Jae-eun moved to Japan in 1975 and became absorbed in the unconventional Sogetsu Ikebana at the Sogetsu Art Center, which was the birthplace of Japanese avant-garde art at the time. He studied under Teshigahara Sofu and Teshigahara Hiroshi2 and fully experienced the period of change when avant-garde ikebana expanded from indoor space to the ground, adding depth to the world of his work. Afterwards, the artist continued his activities on the international stage, including participating as the representative artist of the Japanese Pavilion at the Venice Biennale (1995), participating in the Sao Paulo Biennale (1991), and being invited to the main exhibition at the Venice Biennale Architecture Exhibition (2016). Additionally, in 《Grand Tea Ceremony in Paris》 (1993), together with Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, Tadao Ando, etc., the tea room 〈Another Moons〉 was presented in the ‘Garden of Peace’ at the UNESCO headquarters in Paris, and was presented to major international audiences. We have established a solid position through the project. In Korea, he carried out various public projects such as 〈Synchronous〉(1990) at Gyeongdong Church in Seoul, 〈Seon Space〉(1995–1998) at the Monk Seongcheol Stupa at Haeinsa Temple, and 〈Direction of Time〉(1994) at Samsung Seoul Hospital. He is also well known for his long-term project that expanded “Dreaming of Earth Project” (2015– ) into “Nature Rules” (2020– ). The title 《Promise (Where Beings Be)》, like the artist's expression of 'coexistence and covenant (共生之約)', goes beyond linguistic meaning and is presented as a concept that reminds us of the mutual solidarity of nature that has penetrated time and space long before civilization. Just as the origins of ‘weak’ and ‘genus’ are tied together, Beings have literally been intertwined like a skein of thread and have been placed together throughout time. This exhibition is composed of the subthemes of ‘Lucy’, ‘Light Bell’, ‘Microcosm’, ‘Unknown’, and ‘Natural State: Beyond Boundaries’, and an archive that provides a view of the artist’s major works is also presented. The exhibition, which summons the long axis of time shared between the first humans and the present, and reveals the responsibility humans must bear for the destruction of nature and life, evokes the possibility of symbiosis through bleached corals, life in the DMZ, and disappearing wild flowers, and leads to the path of ecological solidarity proposed by the artist. In a rapidly changing global environment, “Choi Jae-eun: Promise” asks what kind of life we ​​should pursue. -1 Ikebana is a traditional Japanese flower arrangement art, and Sogetsu Ikebana is one of the Ikebana schools.2 Teshigahara Sofu and Teshigahara Hiroshi - The founder and successor of Sogetsu-ryu, leading the expansion and experimentation of avant-garde Ikebana. title: 2025-2026 Jeonnam Provincial Museum of Art Media Collection Exhibition
venue: Jeonnam | Jeonnam Provincial Museum of Art
description: Jeonnam Provincial Museum of Art has played a social role in sharing the cultural value of a public art museum by collecting major works of contemporary art and sharing them with local residents. This media collection exhibition “Data and Artificial Intelligence, Imaginary Landscape, Fictional Narrative” presents works by ‘Tahn’, ‘Kim Chang-gyeom’, and ‘Rinus Van de Velde’ among the media art works collected by the museum, and looks at the ways in which contemporary media art newly constructs reality through technology and imagination. The three artists introduced in the exhibition propose a journey that crosses the border between reality and imagination by building a new world in their own ways: ‘data and artificial intelligence’, ‘imaginary landscape’, and ‘fictional narrative’. Tian uses data and artificial intelligence technology to reconstruct the natural landscape of Jeollanam-do, presenting a new landscape painting in which visible landscapes and invisible data layers coexist. Kim Chang-gyeom creates imaginary landscapes with 3D digital images, unfolding a dreamlike world where reality and fantasy intersect. Linus van de Velde builds his own virtual worldview through an imaginary narrative starting from a day in the life of a 20th century plein air artist. The three authors of Data and Artificial Intelligence, Imaginary Landscapes, and Fictional Narratives each overcome the boundaries of reality in their own way, presenting new possibilities in the way we experience and understand the world. Through this exhibition, we hope to look at the world we live in from a new perspective and experience the power of technology and imagination to enrich reality. title: Special exhibition of Goam Lee Eungno Birthplace Memorial Hall collection 《Expanding Line》
venue: Chungnam | Goam Lee Ungno Birthplace Memorial Hall
description: Goam Lee Ungno’s world of art can be viewed as a journey of a ‘line’ that goes beyond one person’s life and penetrates times and thoughts. For him, line was not just a starting point for formative work, but a way to view and understand the world, and an important form of expression that linked life and art. From ink and drawing in the early stages, to experimentation with materials and transformation of letter forms in the middle period, to group work in the final stage, Goam's works have built a unique formative world, crossing the boundaries of time, place, material and form. The 2025 Goam Lee Ungno Birthplace Memorial Hall collection special exhibition “Expanding Lines” examines Goam’s journey through the flow of ‘thinking lines – changing lines – forming lines – expanding lines’, and is an opportunity to encounter the various aspects of lines and formative changes revealed in the works of each period. By comparing lines expressed in different ways, visitors can naturally experience the flow of how an artist expanded his world. title: Han Yeong-suk style Lee Cheol-jin dance: Seungmu only
description:
[Performance introduction]

Every Monday in 2026,
Held at Sungkyun Small Theater in Daehakro
Lee Cheol-jin’s story of Seungmu, “Only Seungmu”.


Seungmu (僧舞) is a work of art that represents Korean traditional dance and is a highly aesthetic dance that captures both the spirituality of Buddhist practice and human inner emotions. Jang Sam's delicate lines, controlled breathing and rhythm, and aesthetics of still movement create a world of vitality and deep thought that explodes in silence.

 
This stage is a Seungmu dance presented through an in-depth interpretation by Lee Cheol-jin, a dancer who continues the orthodox lineage that runs from Han Seong-jun, Han Young-sook, and Lee Ae-ju. Having walked a single path as a Buddhist monk for decades, he fully displays the philosophy of dance and the density of time on the stage. In each movement and breath, the accumulated traces of practice and the artist's skills are clearly revealed.

 
〈Only Seungmu〉, which is held as an open run, provides a special time for the audience to face their own inner self through the echo of movement that resonates in silence.

title: 2026 Lee Ungno Museum Special Exhibition 《Lee Jong-su-Clay, Play, Stay》
venue: Daejeon | Daejeon Lee Ungno Art Museum
description: Soil holds the memories of the land, and fire breathes new life into those memories. Lee Jong-su's (1935–2008) ceramics capture the journey of an artist's gaze and fingertips who have encountered nature for over half a century, using the two elements of earth and fire. His work was formed on the soil and climate of the region, and on the materials he had accumulated throughout his life, and this ceramic art exhibition reflects not only that material foundation, but also the spiritual and aesthetic soil that underlies it. Lee Jong-su's ceramic art respects the physical properties of soil and the sense of time inherent in it, and contains an attitude of carefully examining the actions of fire and air. He accepted the flow of glaze, changes during firing, and differences in surface texture that appear during the production process as a single result, and paid attention to the state created by materials and processes together. This approach gives each piece a different expression and leaves traces of time and environment on the surface of the ceramics. Rather than a technique for perfecting a form, his work is closer to the accumulation of a long-term relationship with the material called earth. Meanwhile, his work is based on the form of traditional ceramics, but shows formative flexibility that is not overly bound by norms. Subtle changes in proportion, uneven treatment of the surface, and gentle deviations in form simultaneously provide tension and space to the work. These characteristics reflect contemporary sensibility within the framework of the inheritance of tradition, and position his objects not as decorative objects but as formative beings that cross the boundaries between use and appreciation. This attitude implicitly resonates with the work of Goam Lee Ungno (1904–1989), who accepted nature not as an ‘object to be drawn’ but as a place where energy and rhythm flow. Based on the sense of East Asian aesthetics that calligraphy and painting come from the same root, Ungno Lee has expanded brushstrokes not to ‘reproduction of form’ but to traces left by movement and breathing. The free strokes and lively energy seen in his character abstract and group portrait series are revealed through trust in the density created by action rather than precise control of the screen. Lee Jong-su’s ceramic art is also formed based on this awareness. He watched the process of earth, fire, air, and time interacting with each other until the end, and accepted the changes that emerged during the production process as part of the work rather than prescribing the result. Rather than aiming for perfect control, his sculpture is closer to the way materials and processes work together to create form. At this point, the two artists, while handling different materials such as ink and paper, earth and fire, share an attitude of respecting and responding to the nature and flow of the materials. The form is not a product of planning, but is gradually elongated over time when materials and actions intersect. The exhibition title 《Clay, Play, Stay》 concisely reveals Jongsu Lee's world of work. Clay is the soil that is the source of existence that he has studied throughout his life, and Play is a continuous process of exploration in which he tests and adjusts forms in the rhythm of hands, time, and fire. Stay refers to the place where accumulated time remains, and refers not to the completed object staying at a fixed moment, but to the layers of sensation that permeate the surface and form. In Lee Jong-su's ceramics, the form is not decided right away. Through the repetition of creating, repairing, and rebuilding, the form gradually acquires an outline, and the process itself becomes a part of the work. This repetition is not only a formative experiment, but also reveals the life attitude of an artist who has had a long-term relationship with the material called earth. 《Clay, Play, Stay》 follows the process of work that begins with clay and eventually leads to the time of stay, quietly revealing the material depth and meaning of accumulation in Lee Jong-soo's ceramic art. This concept of ‘stay’ goes beyond the level of the work and extends to the artist’s life and the time of the region. 2026 is the first year that the ‘Lee Jong-su Ceramic Museum’ opened its doors in Daejeon, and this retrospective exhibition clearly refers to the work of Daejeon-born artist Lee Jong-su from its starting point. His formative language, formed in the local soil and climate, is now facing the time to accumulate while staying in one place. title: Yoo Seon-Tae’s Invitational Exhibition ‘My Garden, My Artelier’
description: Yoo Seon-tae's invitation exhibition 'My Garden, My Artelier' January 28 (Wed) - March 7 (Sat) Hall II: Gallery Gaia Busan T. 051-627-3373 (16 2F, Daeyeon-dong, Nam-gu, Busan) Opening hours: Tue~Sat 11am~4pm (reservations on public holidays) March 17 (Wed)~May 30 (Sat) Hall I: Gallery Gaia Seoul T. 02-733-3373 (80-5 1F, Cheongdam-dong, Gangnam-gu, Seoul) Opening hours: Tue~Sat 11am~6pm (reservations on public holidays) <Introduction of the artist and description of the work> Artist Seontae Yoo studied at Hongik University, the same graduate school, and the National University of Fine Arts in Paris. After receiving his doctorate from the University of Paris VIII, he held numerous solo exhibitions in Seoul, Paris, New York, Belgium, Spain, etc. He is attracting attention for his lyrical surrealism that uses acrylic, a Western painting material, along with the principles of Oriental painting. The artist, who works across three-dimensional and two-dimensional surfaces, describes his work as a 'forest of objects' and creates mysterious scenes in a space that transcends inside and outside, reality and fantasy, using so many familiar objects from everyday life. Artist Yoo Seon-tae's paintings utilize the technique of 'dépaysement', which places objects in unfamiliar relationships, that is, drawing or arranging everyday objects differently from their intended use to make the viewer feel unfamiliar. By reconstructing various objects in a surreal three-dimensional space, the artist enables new changes in perception and enjoyable imagination. title: Poetics of Extinction: About the Art of Perishing
venue: Seoul | National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul
description: An outstanding work is called an immortal masterpiece. In this case, immortal means incorruptible. If a great work is one that will not or should not change anytime soon, why bother creating a work that will change and then disappear? «Poetics of Extinction: About Decaying Art» introduces works that acknowledge the fate of decaying one day, works that decide not to leave behind anything, and works that openly stage their own decomposition, all under the name of 'decaying art'. This is to look at the changing aspects of work along with today's explosive criticism of anthropocentrism and the backlash against cutting-edge capitalism and technological omnipotence, and to seek wisdom to overcome the current crisis. The Korean word 'sakda' contains the meanings of 'become rotten' and 'lose vitality' as well as 'digested' and 'fermented to taste.' This word provides a valid path to interpreting changes in today's works. This is because it goes beyond the negative connotations contained in the expression ‘rotten’ and encompasses both the descent and rise of energy, and reminds us of the qualitative enhancement achieved through cooperation with non-human beings, such as fermentation. What happens when ‘works’ as evidence of creative human beings disappear? If grass grows where the ‘work’ is destroyed, the wind blows, and invisible life begins to move, can we call it a ‘work’ again? Whose ‘work’ then? As a repository of timeless masterpieces, the museum has been dedicated to preserving the value of great works. The art of sacrificing is asking. Are you ready to accept a work in which you have decided to sacrifice yourself in order to live with various beings beyond humans? Today, as the suspicious season continues, can we admit that it is time to think about how to decompose better rather than preserve better? title: Special Exhibition 《Moment of Expansion: Seolbak·Lee Seong-kyung》
venue: Jeonnam | Hampyeong County Museum of Art
description: Every year, the Hampyeong County Museum of Art continues to hold special exhibitions that highlight young artists who have accumulated meaningful achievements in the flow of contemporary art and formed their own world of work. This is based on the museum's long-term planning direction that goes beyond simply discovering new artists and examines the density of work formed over a certain period of time and practice as well as its future possibilities. 《Moment of Expansion: Seolbak and Lee Seong-kyung》 is an extension of this annual project and focuses on the present of two artists who are on the border between accumulation and leap forward. Lee Seong-kyung's paintings often feature scenes of unclear boundaries where day and night, presence and absence intersect, like shadows at sunset. He focuses on the moment when the outline of an object becomes blurred, and places overlapping viewpoints within a single screen, like a landscape beyond a glass window or a reflected image. This method reflects the artist's attitude of trying to reveal the world in its shaky state rather than clearly dividing it. His work leads the viewer to a borderline space where senses and emotions are condensed. Seolbak is an artist who took the materials and thoughts of traditional Korean ink painting as a starting point and expanded them in a contemporary way. He has continued to conduct a variety of formal experiments ranging from collage, installation, and abstraction, focusing on the material called food, and recognizes nature not as an external object but as a condition to which he belongs and a metaphor for his senses. His work unfolds with an attitude of converting the energy and vitality of nature into the language of the present rather than tension with tradition. Rather than presenting a completed result, 《Moment of Expansion: Seolbak and Lee Seong-kyung》 shows both the density of creativity that the writers have reached at this point and the direction of possibilities that will unfold thereafter. Hampyeong County Museum of Art, through its annual special exhibition of young artists, seeks to read the accumulated texture of time and seek the next landscape for contemporary art, rather than defining the artist as a single stage. title: Anthony McCall: Lines that Draw a Cone 2.0
description: .“Where is the work? Is it on the wall? On the floor? In space? Or am I the work?” The exhibition “Line Drawing a Cone 2.0” focuses on Anthony McCall’s Solid Light work and highlights his world of work that crosses the boundaries of film, sculpture, and installation. A moving line of light slowly crosses space, creating a cone-like shape, and the process appears as an event created in time rather than as a fixed result. He began his work in the early 1970s through a film project called ‘Expanded Cinema’, and in 1973 he presented ‘Line Drawing a Cone’, a work using cigarette smoke and a 16mm projector. A single line drawing projected on the wall formed a huge cone shape in space, but it was difficult to continue this work due to the stereotypes and technical limitations of the time. He stopped working for about 20 years, and in the early 2000s, he entered another turning point by converting his film work to digital files. Technological shifts affected not only the form of the work but also its philosophical depth. The white noise produced by the film projector has disappeared, allowing visitors to focus more on their bodies, senses, and inner self. Simple line animation has evolved into rhythmic drawing lines, and the fog filled with cigarette smoke has been replaced with a haze machine, revealing a clearer light structure. The most notable change in his work since the 2000s is that the viewer's physical intervention is more actively required. The viewer no longer stays in front of the screen, but is guided into the cone-shaped structure formed by light. The body facing the work appears cut or divided by the light. The basic act of the viewer existing, moving, and moving within the space becomes a part of the work. Here, light is no longer an object to look at, but acts as an experience that the body perceives as it passes through it. 〈Line Drawing a Cone 2.0〉 is not an exhibition that presents a completed shape. The exhibition allows you to encounter the process of drawing light, place your body within it, and directly experience the forms that are created and disappear in time. At this time, the work is not formed on the screen, but within the viewer's body, senses, and the space of that moment. title: 19th Venice Biennale International Architecture Exhibition Korean Pavilion Returning Exhibition 《Thick, Thick: Time at Home》
description: The Korean Pavilion exhibition at the 19th Venice Biennale International Architecture Exhibition explores the architecture of the Korean Pavilion, which has celebrated its 30th anniversary. The meaning of the pavilion, which has been used in numerous exhibitions so far, is reexamined from the perspective of ‘home’. This exhibition explores the future of the Korean Pavilion by highlighting its founding and past. The exhibition consists of research and visuals that trigger awareness of these issues by viewing the pavilion not as a neutral exhibition site but as an organic living thing with multi-layered meaning. ‘Thick, Thick, Thick’, taken from a traditional Korean children’s song, is a metaphorical framework for explaining these contents. ‘Thick, Thick’ is a house-building song sung while playing with dirt, reminiscent of Grotto, the primitive form of poly. The toad, the hidden speaker of the exhibition, symbolizes change and regeneration and evokes the old common legacies of Giardini Park, such as trees, land, sky, and sea. The homecoming exhibition held at the Arko Art Museum in Seoul was newly organized under different conditions from those in Venice. The first floor exhibition consists of materials related to the Korean pavilion's architecture and exhibition history and critically edited works, and serves as a public forum where related programs are held. The second floor exhibition examines how participating artists interpreted the conditions of the Korean pavilion and expanded it from a post-national perspective. The site-specific installation works shown in Venice are reorganized in a way that reveals the process and strategy during the return exhibition, and the audience experiences the exhibition along various paths of interpretation and practice.
